open_obligations: Note that the judge is an LLM fine-tuned on human judgements, not a human judge.
Check whether the debaters actually produced refutations in the second turn.
Check confidence intervals on the 2-point debate versus double-consultancy gap.
out.other_title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?
out.rationale: Parrish et al. suggest debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that reference the other side. Arnesen et al. report debate 77% versus double consultancy 75% (both sides shown, no refutation) and that one-turn debates are judged as accurately as two-turn ones, concluding either debaters fail to refute meaningfully or the judge does not benefit; the judge is an LLM, not a human.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether refutation between sides adds value over independent arguments, for trained Llama3-8B debaters and a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo judge on QuALITY-HARD

open_obligations: Note that Arnesen et al.'s judge is an LLM and Michael et al.'s are humans.
Check whether Arnesen et al.'s debaters actually engaged in refutation.
Check whether Michael et al.'s interactive consultancy is comparable to Arnesen et al.'s non-interactive single consultancy.

Note that Arnesen et al.'s debaters and consultants are trained language models, with accuracy reported across checkpoints (for example 72% across all checkpoints for ensembled consultancy), and check whether Michael et al.'s consultants were humans rather than models.
Note that Michael et al.'s 52% is a share of consultancy mistakes, not a judge accuracy like Arnesen et al.'s figures.
out.other_title: Consultancy errors: 52% from failing to extract key evidence from a dishonest consultant
out.rationale: Michael et al. report that 52% of consultancy mistakes involve judges not getting key evidence from a dishonest consultant, and attribute consultancy's omitted key evidence to there being no opponent to call out misrepresentation of the evidence or to provide contradictory evidence. Arnesen et al. report double consultancy, where both sides' speeches are shown but never see each other, reaches 75% versus debate 77% (single consultancy 68%), suggesting most of the gain comes from seeing both sides rather than refutation. Because double consultancy shows the judge both sides without letting either side see the other's arguments, the result bears only on the call-out (refutation) part of Michael et al.'s explanation, not on the provision of contradictory evidence; judges are a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo, not humans.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate's advantage over consultancy comes from an opponent calling out misrepresented evidence

text: The paper reports judge accuracy of 72% for ensembled consultancy versus 68% for single consultancy, 75% for double consultancy and 77% for debate. Because double consultancy comes close to debate although the sides never see each other's arguments, the authors conclude that either the debaters fail to engage in meaningful refutation or the judge does not benefit from reading refutations, and they report one-turn debates are judged as accurately as two-turn debates.
title: Judge accuracy: debate 77%, double consultancy 75%, ensembled 72%, single consultancy 68%
